title: Durable, non-destructive seizure freedom in drug-resistant epilepsy

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that reliably gives people with drug-resistant epilepsy lasting freedom from seizures while preserving functional brain tissue, cognition and everyday abilities. Its defining outcome is seizure freedom with functional preservation. The concept leaves the treatment mechanism open.

Two outcomes require separate evaluation. Durable seizure freedom can persist while a treatment remains active. A permanent-cure claim additionally requires evidence that seizure freedom persists after active treatment has stopped. Continued benefit from an implanted device or another ongoing therapy can satisfy a meaningful treatment goal, while treatment-free persistence remains a further capability to demonstrate.

The candidate’s clinical rationale is that seizure-generating networks may be distributed, change over time or involve areas essential for memory, language and movement. Those possibilities explain the proposed emphasis on selective control and functional preservation. The supplied evidence does not independently substantiate these clinical assertions, so they remain an unverified rationale within this record.

significance.text: The conditional significance is substantial. Reliable, lasting seizure freedom with preserved cognition and acceptable safety would directly address the treatment goal for people whose seizures persist despite medication. The proposed advance would combine control of seizures with preservation of the abilities that make treatment worthwhile to the person receiving it.

As a downstream possibility, sustained seizure freedom could improve participation in daily activities and quality of life. These benefits would need measurement alongside seizure outcomes. Prevention of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy or later cognitive decline would require direct evidence, because seizure control alone cannot establish either effect.

The impact depends on breadth, durability and treatment burden. Success in a particular focal epilepsy population would establish benefit within that population. Broader claims would require evidence across additional epilepsy types and patient groups. Treatment-free persistence would extend the significance further, although prolonged observation would still leave uncertainty about recurrence over a lifetime.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability is dependable, sustained seizure freedom in drug-resistant epilepsy with preservation of brain function and acceptable long-term safety. For the stronger permanent-cure version, the capability must include persistence after withdrawal or removal of the active treatment. The supplied evidence cannot establish that either capability has been achieved across the proposed clinical scope.

As an engineering synthesis of the candidate’s rationale, the central challenge is selective intervention. A treatment would need to control the activity responsible for seizures while preserving activity needed for memory, language, movement and other functions. If the relevant networks are distributed or change over time, identifying sufficient treatment targets and maintaining effective control become additional barriers. The supplied material offers no scientific text with which to assess particular mechanisms or solutions.

As a proposed translational framework, development must also resolve how to distinguish incomplete seizure suppression, sustained freedom maintained by ongoing therapy and persistence after treatment cessation. Long-term evaluation must account for recurrence, cognitive effects, quality of life and treatment-related harms. Withdrawal testing introduces a further practical boundary because its feasibility and safety would depend on the intervention and the participant’s circumstances.

current_state.text: The research and source index identify a report attributed to Nair and colleagues in 2020, titled “Nine-year prospective efficacy and safety of brain-responsive neurostimulation for focal epilepsy.” The research describes sustained seizure reductions during long-term treatment. However, the retained artifact examined in the supplied review contains only a cookie-access message, with no authors, title, abstract or results. Consequently, the reported nine-year duration, study identity and clinical findings cannot be independently verified from that artifact. Nine years is the follow-up duration attributed to the cited report, with verification remaining unresolved.

The earlier claim that an indexed abstract supported the characterization exceeds the evidence retained for review. The supplied review found no abstract or results. Although the source index marks the artifact as saved and verified and records an untruncated extraction, those metadata do not establish that the scientific document was accessible. The access barrier leaves the report’s findings unresolved here and provides no evidence against their validity.

The clinical interpretation also requires two distinctions. A reduction in seizure frequency does not establish seizure freedom. Even demonstrated seizure freedom during active treatment would leave treatment-free persistence to be tested separately. These distinctions determine what a successful neurostimulation result could establish about the proposed innovation.

No freshness searches or additional inspectable clinical evidence were supplied. This record therefore cannot establish the field’s state as of the review’s November 1, 2026 reference date or the November 11, 2026 artifact retrieval date. It also cannot determine whether newer studies have demonstrated broader seizure freedom, treatment-free persistence or further safety outcomes.

completion_criteria.text: A proposed convincing demonstration would use controlled trials with independent replication across several clearly specified drug-resistant epilepsy types. Protocols would define the eligible populations, seizure categories, observation methods and duration required for sustained seizure freedom. They would report the proportion achieving freedom and the timing of recurrence, alongside seizure-frequency outcomes, so the claimed capability can be evaluated directly.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled trials independently replicate sustained seizure freedom across epilepsy types

completion_criteria.text: Functional preservation would require prospectively specified assessments of cognition and relevant abilities, together with quality-of-life measures and long-term safety follow-up. Proposed protocols should define acceptable harms, meaningful functional changes, treatment burden and handling of missing follow-up before outcomes are assessed. These are proposed evaluation requirements, with numerical thresholds and durations still to be determined.
completion_criteria.label: Functional preservation demonstrated through prospective assessments and long-term safety follow-up

completion_criteria.text: A permanent-cure claim would require prolonged observation after the active treatment has been discontinued or removed, where that can be evaluated safely. The protocol would need to specify concurrent medications and other active treatments, as well as how recurrence and rescue treatment are handled. Any residual intervention capable of sustaining seizure control would need consideration when interpreting treatment-free persistence. Even a long seizure-free interval would support persistence over the observed period while leaving lifetime permanence uncertain.
completion_criteria.label: Seizure freedom persists after treatment withdrawal over prolonged observation

completion_criteria.text: Independent replication should establish whether the outcome survives differences in clinical teams, settings and patient populations. Reports should identify the epilepsy types, functional regions and treatment histories actually represented, along with exclusions and failures. Finite trials can demonstrate breadth within those boundaries. Broader applicability would require additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication confirms outcomes across reported clinical settings and populations

related_concepts.text: Conceptual relationship to NRL-02, “A general predictive theory of neural circuit computation,” and NRL-03, “Whole-brain, cellular-resolution recording during natural behavior.” Predictive circuit models and detailed recording could help explain seizure-generating networks and identify intervention targets. NRL-14 is defined by a clinical outcome, and its success does not inherently require either roster entry to be completed in full.

Conceptual relationship to NRL-10, “Safe, programmable delivery to selected cells throughout the human brain.” Selective delivery could become an enabling capability for a cell-targeted epilepsy treatment. NRL-10 concerns delivery precision and safety across the brain, while NRL-14 additionally requires demonstrated seizure freedom and preserved function in the treated population.

Conceptual relationship to NRL-17, “A durable bidirectional neural interface for movement and sensation.” An epilepsy intervention using responsive sensing and stimulation would share challenges in long-term recording, stimulation, tissue compatibility and device reliability. The clinical endpoints remain distinct, with NRL-17 addressing movement and sensation and NRL-14 addressing seizure freedom.

Conceptual relationship to NRL-04, “Read and selectively repair the physical traces of specific memories,” and NRL-06, “Replace lost brain tissue while preserving learned function.” These entries share an interest in preserving or recovering learned function during brain intervention. NRL-14 makes functional preservation a constraint on seizure treatment, while memory-trace repair and tissue replacement remain separate capabilities with their own completion criteria.

unresolved_issues: An inspectable scientific copy is needed to verify the cited report’s identity, nine-year follow-up, quantitative efficacy, safety findings and applicability.
The supplied material does not independently substantiate the clinical assertions about distributed or changing seizure networks and involvement of essential functional areas.
No supplied freshness search establishes developments through November 2026.
Trial populations, seizure-freedom duration, ascertainment methods, functional thresholds, acceptable harms and replication requirements remain unspecified.
The feasibility and safety of treatment withdrawal, and the interpretation of residual treatment effects, depend on the eventual intervention.
Mortality and later cognitive-decline benefits remain separate empirical questions.

brief.title: Lasting seizure freedom without harming brain function
possible: People whose epilepsy persists despite medication could live free of seizures while keeping their memory, language, movement and everyday abilities. A treatment would preserve functioning brain tissue while reliably stopping seizures.
Seizure freedom could last while treatment continues. A further goal would be for it to persist after treatment stops.
why: For people whose medicines do not stop seizures, success would mean gaining seizure control while preserving the abilities that make treatment worthwhile.
Sustained seizure freedom could help people participate more fully in daily activities and improve their quality of life.

sources.showed: They reported sustained seizure reductions during long-term treatment with brain-responsive neurostimulation, which uses a device to stimulate the brain in response to its activity.
sources.cited_for: The study supports the possibility of sustained seizure reduction with ongoing device treatment.
sources.not_established: Fewer seizures do not establish lasting seizure freedom or persistence after treatment stops.

sources.showed: Cenobamate, a seizure medicine added to existing drugs, produced seizure-free periods in some adults whose seizures began in one brain region.
sources.cited_for: The controlled trial shows that added medication can achieve seizure freedom during a treatment period.
sources.not_established: A short seizure-free period does not establish durable freedom, preserved brain function or benefit after treatment stops.

sources.who: Tianqi Hu, Hutao Xie, Ming Shan and colleagues
sources.showed: A small study looking back at patients treated with deep brain stimulation, electrical stimulation inside the brain, found fewer seizures, stable thinking abilities and improved quality of life. Some patients had seizure-free periods.
sources.quote: Mood conditions (measured by the Hamilton Depression and Anxiety Rating Scales) improved from baseline to the final follow-up, while cognitive status remained stable.
sources.cited_for: The study links ongoing brain stimulation with seizure reduction and stable scores on tests of thinking abilities.
sources.not_established: This small retrospective study does not establish dependable seizure freedom, full functional preservation or treatment-free persistence.

shown: Chung and colleagues found that 28.3% of adults receiving added cenobamate were seizure-free during the trial's maintenance period, when the dose stayed steady. This demonstrates seizure freedom during treatment over a limited interval.

Hu and colleagues reported seizure-free periods lasting at least six months in some patients receiving brain stimulation. Their small study also found stable thinking abilities and improved quality of life.
missing: A treatment must reliably sustain seizure freedom while preserving functioning brain tissue and everyday abilities.
Long-term studies must establish acceptable harms and treatment burden alongside seizure outcomes.
The combined benefits must hold across different epilepsy types, patient groups and clinical settings.
For a permanent-cure claim, seizure freedom must persist after active treatment stops.

milestones.label: Controlled trials repeatedly find lasting seizure freedom across epilepsy types
milestones.explanation: Independent controlled trials would have to reproduce sustained seizure freedom across clearly defined epilepsy types that resist medication. This would establish who benefits and how reliably.

milestones.label: Long-term assessments confirm preserved abilities and acceptable safety
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to track thinking, everyday abilities, quality of life and harms using assessments chosen beforehand. This would establish whether seizure control preserves the functions people value.

milestones.label: Seizure freedom continues after active treatment stops
milestones.explanation: Prolonged observation after safely stopping active treatment would have to show continued seizure freedom, accounting for other therapies. This would support persistence without ongoing treatment.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce outcomes across settings and patient groups
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the outcomes across the clinical settings and patient groups claimed. This would establish how broadly the treatment works beyond its initial trials.

uncertain: How long must seizure freedom last, and what changes in abilities or treatment harms would count as acceptable?
Can treatment safely stop, and could lingering treatment effects explain continued seizure freedom?
Even prolonged seizure freedom after treatment stops would leave lifetime recurrence uncertain.

page.title: Seizure freedom with preserved function in drug-resistant epilepsy
page.definition: A treatment stops all seizures after adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication regimens have failed, without removing or intentionally destroying brain tissue or causing clinically meaningful loss of cognition or everyday function. Continued treatment may be necessary.

goal.need: In Lecco, Italy, 107 of 684 people with active epilepsy (15.6%) had drug-resistant epilepsy. In a prospective study of adults with focal epilepsy, 11.8% achieved sustained seizure freedom with another medication after two drugs had failed. Even one seizure a year can restrict driving. Lasting seizure freedom can improve quality of life and help people regain eligibility to drive. Preserving memory matters too: temporal lobe surgery can control seizures but can impair verbal memory.

completion.title: A controlled trial establishes sustained seizure freedom with preserved function.
completion.criterion: A randomized controlled trial in a prespecified drug-resistant epilepsy population demonstrates superiority over control on a registered joint endpoint: no seizures, including auras, for at least 12 months or three times the longest pretreatment seizure interval during the preceding 12 months, whichever is longer, together with no clinically meaningful deterioration in cognition, language, motor function or everyday functioning under prespecified reliable-change or noninferiority criteria. The intervention neither removes nor intentionally destroys brain tissue. Ongoing treatment is permitted. Success is assessed separately by epilepsy type.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of ILAE seizure-outcome definitions, AES/NINDS research goals and clinical trial methodology; no outside body identified with this combined test.
completion.basis: The ILAE defines sustained seizure freedom for each patient. The EMA guideline for add-on drug trials treats functional outcomes and quality of life as additional endpoints. The Atlas combines these requirements: each responder must meet both the seizure and functional criteria, and the trial must establish superiority over control on that joint outcome. The functional measures and margins must be specified in advance. The endpoint permits continued treatment.

milestones.title: A compound prevents the defining seizure signs in an acute mouse screening test.
milestones.criterion: In the maximal-electroshock test, the mouse shows no tonic extension of the hindlimbs after a 50 mA, 60 Hz corneal stimulus lasting 0.2 seconds. In the alternative 6 Hz test, the mouse shows none of the defining signs after a 44 mA corneal stimulus lasting 3 seconds: momentary stunning, rhythmic forelimb jerking, whisker twitching or rigid elevation of the tail. Both tests assess an induced seizure in an otherwise neurologically intact mouse.
milestones.set_by: NINDS Epilepsy Therapy Screening Program, published 2017 validation protocol. These criteria were written for compounds in generalized-convulsive and focal-seizure models.
milestones.threshold_quote: An animal was considered “protected” from MES-induced seizures in the absence of the hindlimb tonic extension component of the seizure

milestones.title: An epilepsy intervention is administered to patients in an authorized feasibility study.
milestones.criterion: Patients with drug-resistant epilepsy receive the investigational intervention under an authorized feasibility protocol that evaluates preliminary safety and effectiveness. For an implanted system, the study must document implantation.
milestones.set_by: FDA, RNS System Summary of Safety and Effectiveness Data, feasibility-study stage. The documented study concerned focal epilepsy.
milestones.threshold_quote: A Feasibility study was performed to evaluate preliminary safety and effectiveness

milestones.title: For focal RNS, upper bounds on serious-event rates are below 20% at 4 weeks and 42% at 12 weeks.
milestones.criterion: In implanted patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy, calculate the one-sided 95% Wilson upper confidence limit for the proportion with at least one serious adverse event, irrespective of attribution. Count from implantation through week 4 and separately from implantation through week 12. The upper limits must be below the corresponding historical comparator bounds of 20% and 42%.
milestones.set_by: NeuroPace RNS pivotal protocol for focal epilepsy, as reviewed by FDA in Table 14 and its footnotes
milestones.threshold_quote: Upper limit for the RNS® System is less than that of the comparator.

milestones.title: An add-on treatment reduces 28-day seizure frequency more than placebo in a randomized trial.
milestones.criterion: Compare the percentage change from baseline in seizure frequency per 28 days between randomized add-on treatment and placebo during double-blind treatment, including titration and maintenance. Demonstrate a statistically greater reduction with treatment for the seizure types specified in the protocol. The focal protocol counts qualifying focal seizures. The idiopathic generalized epilepsy protocol counts primary generalized tonic–clonic seizures.
milestones.set_by: Cenobamate trial NCT01397968 and perampanel Study 332, NCT01393743
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary outcome was percent change in seizure frequency (from baseline) per 28 days during double-blind treatment.

milestones.title: Seizure freedom lasts ≥12 months and ≥3 times the patient’s longest pretreatment seizure interval.
milestones.criterion: For each patient, determine the longest interval between seizures during the 12 months before treatment. Document freedom from every seizure type, including auras, for at least 12 months and at least three times that pretreatment interval. A fixed year of follow-up suffices only when the longest pretreatment interval was four months or less.
milestones.set_by: ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies, 2010 consensus definition and glossary; applicable across epilepsy types.
milestones.threshold_quote: 12 months or three times the preintervention interseizure interval, whichever is longer

milestones.title: A compound limits an evoked seizure to stage 3 or lower in a fully kindled mouse.
milestones.criterion: In the NINDS corneal-kindling assay, a mouse qualifies after five consecutive stage 5 seizures. Testing starts at least 5–7 days after the last stimulation needed to kindle the cohort. After treatment and test stimulation, the mouse must score 3 or lower on the behavioral seizure scale.
milestones.set_by: NINDS Epilepsy Therapy Screening Program, corneal-kindled mouse assay
milestones.threshold_quote: On the testing day, mice displaying a seizure score ≤ 3 were considered protected.

milestones.title: Thalamic RNS has an 84-day serious device-related event rate significantly below 25% in generalized epilepsy.
milestones.criterion: In patients aged 12 years or older with drug-resistant idiopathic generalized epilepsy and at least two generalized tonic–clonic seizures during a three-month baseline, assess serious device-related events through 84 days after implantation of bilateral centromedian thalamic leads. Use a one-sided exact binomial test to establish that the proportion of implanted patients with an event is below 25%.
milestones.threshold_quote: the upper bound of the confidence interval well below the 25% performance goal

milestones.title: Two-year changes in naming and verbal learning are classified using 90% reliable-change limits.
milestones.criterion: Compare each patient’s baseline and two-year scores on the Boston Naming Test and the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. For each measure, report the proportions with reliable decline, no reliable change and reliable improvement under the 90% reliable-change limits. Use the published adjustment for the test form when scoring verbal learning. The limits account for test–retest variation and practice effects.
milestones.set_by: Neuropsychological reliable-change convention applied in the focal-epilepsy RNS follow-up by Loring and colleagues, Table 3
milestones.threshold_quote:
Percent of subjects with 90% RCI changes at
2 years

results.detail: The post hoc model used monthly counts and a negative binomial distribution. The preceding stimulation optimization period was also blinded.
results.quote:
The GEE analysis, with these post hoc modifications, was used to demonstrate 
efficacy.

results.finding: Among 149 focal RNS patients with paired naming scores, the two-year mean change was +1.28 points.
NeuroPace reports completed RNS implantation procedures in a feasibility study that enrolled 20 patients with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and drug-resistant generalized-onset seizures.
results.detail: The release reports completed implant procedures for the study as a whole. The count of 20 is explicitly the enrollment count.
results.quote: Enrollment and implant procedures completed in NIH funded feasibility study of LGS, a severe and disabling childhood-onset epilepsy

results.finding: Adjunctive perampanel reduced median 28-day primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure frequency by 76.5% in a randomized trial of 162 analyzed patients.
results.detail: The supplied text renders the negative changes as “238.4%” and “276.5%”. They are expressed here as reductions, consistent with the article’s description.
results.quote:
Results: Of 164 randomized patients, 162 comprised the full analysis set (placebo, 81; perampa-
nel, 81). Compared with placebo, perampanel conferred a greater median percent change in
PGTC seizure frequency per 28 days ( 238.4% vs 276.5%; p , 0.0001)

results.finding: Among 81 perampanel-treated patients with idiopathic generalized epilepsy, 23.5% were free of all seizures during maintenance.
results.quote:
4.9% of placebo-treated
patients and 23.5% of perampanel-treated patients
achieved freedom from all seizures.

results.finding: After cenobamate add-on, 24 of 50 patients with focal or multifocal epilepsy had at least a 50% reduction in monthly seizure frequency.
results.detail: The focal responder count comes from Table 4. The cohort-wide response rate in the quoted sentence uses all 54 patients.
results.quote: The responder rate was 44.4% (24/54).

results.finding: Among 50 patients with focal or multifocal epilepsy, six reported seizure freedom after cenobamate add-on, with a median duration of 26 weeks.
results.detail: Seizure data came from retrospective patient reports without systematic seizure diaries. Table 4 identifies the epilepsy type of all six seizure-free patients.
results.quote: Of these, six patients (11.1% of the total cohort) achieved seizure freedom at last follow‐up with a median seizure freedom duration of 26 weeks (Q1 16, Q3 51, range 4–60).

results.finding: (R)‐AS‐1 protected male C57BL/6J mice in the acute 6 Hz screen at a median effective dose of 65.9 mg/kg (sample size unstated).
results.detail: The text gives the median effective dose in Table 1 and describes behavioral protection in the Results and Discussion. The case follows the paper’s classification of this screen as a focal seizure model.
results.quote: suppressed 6 Hz seizures at 44 mA in male C57BL/6J mice

results.finding: Fully corneal-kindled male mice were seizure free after (R)‐AS‐1 at 50 mg/kg (sample size unstated).
results.detail: The reported 3–4-day washout applies between dose tests. The criterion specifies a separate 5–7-day minimum interval after the last kindling stimulus.
results.quote: Animals were seizure free at doses of 50 mg/kg (male mice) and 90 mg/kg (female mice).

results.finding: Among 32 adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy receiving add-on cenobamate, 14 met the seizure-frequency responder threshold.
results.detail: Baseline monthly seizure frequency was estimated retrospectively from three months of medical records and seizure diaries.
results.quote:
Fourteen/32 (44%) patients were responders (≥ 50% reduction in seizure 
frequency) to cenobamate

results.finding: Among 32 adults with drug-resistant focal epilepsy receiving add-on cenobamate, 3 reached the minimum seizure-free duration.
results.detail: The study classified patients as seizure-free after 12 months or three times the longest pre-intervention interval. The Atlas requires both duration thresholds.
results.quote:
Of the five seizure-free patients, one patient 
did not present seizures for 27 months, another for 19 
months, and another one for 15 months.

results.finding: In 514 adults with focal epilepsy, adjunctive cenobamate reduced 28-day seizure frequency more than placebo over the full double-blind period (p < .001 for each dose).
results.detail: The full-period comparison was a secondary outcome. The primary outcome covered the 6-week maintenance phase.
results.quote: Median percent reductions in 28‐day focal seizure frequency during the 12‐week treatment period and the entire 24‐week double‐blind treatment period were also significant (all  p 's < .001 vs placebo) for the cenobamate treatment groups compared to placebo (Figure  3B,C ).

results.finding: Among 478 adults with focal epilepsy in the 12-week analysis, 30.6% of the highest-dose cenobamate group had no qualifying focal seizures.
results.detail: The 12-week window covered the final 6 weeks of titration and 6 weeks of maintenance. The study used an 8-week baseline and counted focal aware motor, focal impaired awareness, and focal to bilateral tonic–clonic seizures.
results.quote: Seizure‐free rates during the maintenance phase were 2.6% of patients for placebo vs 12.4%, 30.1%, and 52.4% for cenobamate 100, 200, and 400 mg/day, respectively, and during the 12‐week period were 0.8% for placebo vs 8.5%, 19.7%, and 30.6% for the cenobamate groups.

results.finding: In X-TOLE2 (n=374), add-on azetukalner produced a median 53.2% reduction in 28-day focal seizure frequency at the higher dose, significantly exceeding placebo.
results.quote: The median (IQR) change from baseline in monthly seizure frequency was −10.4% (−39.1% to 8.3%) for the placebo group, −34.5% (−61.6% to −12.3%) for the 15-mg azetukalner group ( P  < .001 vs placebo), and −53.2% (−77.2% to −28.8%) for the 25-mg azetukalner group ( P  < .001 vs placebo).

results.finding: Among 124 adults receiving higher-dose azetukalner in X-TOLE2, 6.5% had zero countable focal seizures throughout double-blind treatment.
results.detail: The 12-month seizure-freedom figures discussed in the paper come from the separate phase 2b X-TOLE open-label extension.
results.quote: for 100% reduction, 1 participant (0.8%), 5 participants (4.0%) ( P  = .12 [nominal] vs placebo), and 8 participants (6.5%) ( P  = .03 [nominal] vs placebo), respectively, were responders.

results.finding: Adjunctive lacosamide in idiopathic generalized epilepsy (n=238): median 88.6% reduction in 28-day tonic–clonic seizure frequency.
results.quote: Median percent change in GTCS frequency per 28 days from the combined baseline was −88.6% (range = −100.0 to 465.4,  n  = 238).

results.finding: Adjunctive lacosamide in idiopathic generalized epilepsy (n=238): 49.6% had at least 12 months free of all reported seizure types.
results.detail: The cohort included patients with only one lifetime antiseizure medication. The study did not establish two adequate regimen failures for the patients who achieved seizure freedom.
results.quote: Overall, 118 (49.6%) patients had ≥12 months freedom from all seizure types at any time during the trial (Figure  S1C ).

results.finding: Among 138 Study 332 extension entrants with idiopathic generalized epilepsy, the median reduction in 28-day generalized tonic–clonic seizure frequency was 90% in weeks 40–52.
results.detail: Participants originally assigned to placebo switched to perampanel during the extension. The extension analysis used descriptive statistics, with no concurrent placebo arm or test of superiority.
results.quote: Median percent reductions in GTC seizures per 28 days from preperampanel were 77% (Weeks 1‐13) and 90% (Weeks 40‐52).

results.finding: Among 68 Study 332 extension entrants with idiopathic generalized epilepsy assigned to perampanel in the core trial, 22.1% were free of all reported seizure types for at least 12 months.
results.detail: The core trial used an eight-week baseline. The analysis counted missing diary days as seizure-free, and diary collection stopped at the start of extension Part B.
results.quote: For all seizure types, 39.7% and 22.1% of patients who received perampanel during the Core Study and 35.7% and 17.1% of patients who received placebo during the Core Study were free from all seizures for at least 6 or 12 months, respectively (Figure  3D ii).

results.finding: Perampanel prevented tonic hindlimb extension in 85.6% of male NIH Swiss mice (n ≥ 8) in the maximal-electroshock test.
results.detail: Figure 1A gives a minimum sample size per time point. The exact denominator for this dose and time point is unspecified in the supplied text.
results.quote:
dose of perampanel (2 mg/kg) conferred nearly complete 
seizure protection (85.6%) at 10 min

results.finding: l-Norfenfluramine prevented tonic hindlimb extension in 100% of CF-1 mice (n = 8).
results.detail: The result is an acute induced-seizure screen. Its applicability to combined generalized and focal epilepsy in patients remains untested by this experiment.

results.finding: After perampanel, all 8 fully corneal-kindled male CF-1 mice in the vehicle-kindled cohort scored Racine stage 2 or lower.
results.detail: Table 2 reports the protection count. The study used a stricter cutoff for protection, Racine stage 2 or lower.

results.finding: All 10 adults with drug-resistant generalized epilepsy received implanted microburst vagus nerve stimulation in the feasibility study.
results.detail: The FDA Investigational Device Exemption described in the paper covered MRI-related procedures. Institutional review board approval covered all study procedures. The safety summary was reported for the overall cohort.
results.quote: Eighteen patients with focal (Foc) and 10 with generalized (Gen) DRE underwent 3T resting‐state fMRI at 2 weeks post‐implantation and before starting (baseline) and after 6 months of μVNS.

results.finding: All 15 analyzed Lennox–Gastaut syndrome feasibility-study participants received two RNS neurostimulator implants each.
results.detail: The seizure recordings selected for expert review were collected with stimulation off.
results.quote: Per trial protocol, participants with LGS received two neurostimulator implants (red arrows), one in each hemisphere.

results.finding: Among 87 patients with drug-resistant idiopathic generalized epilepsy implanted with bilateral centromedian thalamic RNS leads, 6.9% had a serious device-related event by day 84.
results.detail: The implanted cohort ranged from 14 to 66 years of age.
results.quote: The primary safety endpoint was met; the SADE rate at 84 days postimplant was 6.9% (6/87 patients, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 2.9%–14.5%), with the upper bound of the confidence interval well below the 25% performance goal ( p  < .0001).

results.finding: Among 850 adults with confirmed drug-resistant focal epilepsy, 7.6% achieved ILAE-defined seizure freedom after starting another antiseizure medication.
results.quote: The proportion of patients achieving seizure freedom in the PP population was 7.6% based on the EP evaluation

goal.need = "In Lecco, Italy, 107 of 684 people with active epilepsy (15.6%) had drug-resistant epilepsy. In a prospective study of adults with focal epilepsy, 11.8% achieved sustained seizure freedom with another medication after two drugs had failed. Even one seizure a year can restrict driving. Lasting seizure freedom can improve quality of life and help people regain eligibility to drive. Preserving memory matters too: temporal lobe surgery can control seizures but can impair verbal memory.". Reason: The current paragraph gives a trial enrollment count where readers need the size of the affected population and the consequences of persistent seizures and treatment-related memory loss.

add statement by European Medicines Agency, Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, 2025: "However, few patients become seizure-free, which is the ultimate goal of treatment.". Reason: The adopted European guideline explicitly identifies seizure freedom as the goal of drug treatment.

edit completion: basis = "The ILAE defines sustained seizure freedom for each patient. The EMA guideline for add-on drug trials treats functional outcomes and quality of life as additional endpoints. The Atlas combines these requirements: each responder must meet both the seizure and functional criteria, and the trial must establish superiority over control on that joint outcome. The functional measures and margins must be specified in advance. The endpoint permits continued treatment."; refs = [2, 3, 4, 5, 22]. Reason: The basis needs to distinguish the ILAE’s patient-level duration rule, the EMA’s functional assessments and the Atlas requirement that the same participant satisfy both components.

add case "Combined generalized and focal". Reason: The ILAE recognizes combined generalized and focal epilepsy, including presentations of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome, for which a responsive-stimulation feasibility study is already cited.
add case "Unknown epilepsy type". Reason: The ILAE provides an unknown-type category for established epilepsy when the available clinical and EEG evidence is insufficient to classify it further.

edit m1: title = "A compound prevents the defining seizure signs in an acute mouse screening test."; criterion = "In the maximal-electroshock test, the mouse shows no tonic extension of the hindlimbs after a 50 mA, 60 Hz corneal stimulus lasting 0.2 seconds. In the alternative 6 Hz test, the mouse shows none of the defining signs after a 44 mA corneal stimulus lasting 3 seconds: momentary stunning, rhythmic forelimb jerking, whisker twitching or rigid elevation of the tail. Both tests assess an induced seizure in an otherwise neurologically intact mouse.". Reason: The clobazam doses are results, while the stimulus conditions and observable signs define protection in the two assays.

add milestone after m1: "A compound limits an evoked seizure to stage 3 or lower in a fully kindled mouse.". Reason: The screening programme also tests protection after repeated stimulation has made the brain persistently susceptible to seizures, a step the acute assays cannot establish.

edit m2: criterion = "Patients with drug-resistant epilepsy receive the investigational intervention under an authorized feasibility protocol that evaluates preliminary safety and effectiveness. For an implanted system, the study must document implantation."; refs = [4, 11]. Reason: The enrollment date and implant count describe the focal RNS study’s history, while the feasibility milestone turns on patients actually receiving the intervention.

edit m3: title = "For focal RNS, upper bounds on serious-event rates are below 20% at 4 weeks and 42% at 12 weeks."; criterion = "In implanted patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy, calculate the one-sided 95% Wilson upper confidence limit for the proportion with at least one serious adverse event, irrespective of attribution. Count from implantation through week 4 and separately from implantation through week 12. The upper limits must be below the corresponding historical comparator bounds of 20% and 42%."; set_by = "NeuroPace RNS pivotal protocol for focal epilepsy, as reviewed by FDA in Table 14 and its footnotes"; set_by_kind = "protocol"; threshold_quote = "Upper limit for the RNS\u00ae System is less than that of the comparator."; threshold_ref = 4; refs = [4]. Reason: FDA Table 14 specifies a strict comparison of upper confidence limits and the Wilson method, and the limits belong to the focal RNS protocol.

add milestone after m3: "Thalamic RNS has an 84-day serious device-related event rate significantly below 25% in generalized epilepsy.". Reason: The generalized-epilepsy pivotal protocol has its own 84-day safety target and counts only serious device-related events.

edit m4: title = "An add-on treatment reduces 28-day seizure frequency more than placebo in a randomized trial."; criterion = "Compare the percentage change from baseline in seizure frequency per 28 days between randomized add-on treatment and placebo during double-blind treatment, including titration and maintenance. Demonstrate a statistically greater reduction with treatment for the seizure types specified in the protocol. The focal protocol counts qualifying focal seizures. The idiopathic generalized epilepsy protocol counts primary generalized tonic\u2013clonic seizures."; set_by = "Cenobamate trial NCT01397968 and perampanel Study 332, NCT01393743"; refs = [1, 12, 7]. Reason: The two trial protocols specify change from baseline and which seizures count, whereas the current criterion includes their observed reductions and p-values.

add milestone after m4: "Two-year changes in naming and verbal learning are classified using 90% reliable-change limits.". Reason: The milestones need a patient-level measure of cognitive change because a stable group average can conceal declines in individual patients.

edit m5: title = "Seizure freedom lasts \u226512 months and \u22653 times the patient\u2019s longest pretreatment seizure interval."; criterion = "For each patient, determine the longest interval between seizures during the 12 months before treatment. Document freedom from every seizure type, including auras, for at least 12 months and at least three times that pretreatment interval. A fixed year of follow-up suffices only when the longest pretreatment interval was four months or less."; refs = [2, 20, 8, 10]. Reason: The title omits the longer-of rule, and the prospective medication cohort supplies direct evidence for that rule in focal epilepsy.

structure = parallel. Reason: Implant safety, medication efficacy and individual cognitive outcomes can be established independently even though feasibility precedes pivotal testing within a device programme.
